newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom rules stop foreigners buying locally.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom rules stop foreigners buying locally.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin appears to have put an end to foreigners buying cheap shares of wealthy Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, a senior company official said on Wednesday.
But current holders of the bargain stock will not be forced by a new presidential decree to sell, Gazprom securities department director Eduard Ivanov, who saw a draft of the decree, told Reuters.
"We were told it was signed," he said. "If it is released in the version that I saw, foreign investors, non-residents, may not buy shares on the domestic market," he said.
The Kremlin later confirmed that Yeltsin had signed a decree confirming a nine percent cap on foreign share ownership in Gazprom, but was not immediately able to give details.

Gazprom, one of Russia's richest companies which is in the throes of government-ordered reorganisation but jealously guarded from foreigners with a nine percent cap on non-resident ownership, operates a two-tier system for its shares.
Foreigners are required to hold Gazprom in the form of American Depositary Shares (ADSs), share-look alikes which trade abroad at about triple the price of local shares.
But many foreigners, labeled "swindlers" by Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev, have circumvented restrictions by establishing Russian-registered subsidiaries which legally bought local Gazprom shares.
Gazprom says the new rules will make a better market for all investors.
Rumours that foreigners would be told to sell their stock within three months swept the market on Wednesday and Gazprom local share prices were battered by uncertainty.
"They've completely messed up, making it (Gazprom local shares) more unattractive for investors," said one Western trader in Moscow.
Gazprom shares partially recovered to closed at $0.6495 on the Russian Trading System after slipping to $0.6200 midday from Tuesday's $0.6530 close.

Gazprom ADSs, each of which cover 10 underlying shares, rose to $18.250 in London at 1640 GMT from $17.925 at Tuesday's close. The ADS has languished since its launch last October at $15.75, when underlying shares were about $0.50.
Russia will also stop foreigners from issuing securities abroad based on shares held in Russia -- one of the biggest threats to Gazprom's strategy of dividing foreign and domestic markets.

"They may keep them as long as they want but may sell them only on the domestic market," Ivanov said of the domestic shares. "No derivatives, none of their own shares may be issued on the basis of acquired Gazprom shares."
He did say how Russia could stop foreign companies from issuing their own securities.

Gazprom is one of Russia's highest profile and profitable companies, with 1996 sales of 115 trillion roubles ($20 billion), up about 50 percent on a year ago, but it is also one of its most secretive.
The decree would also make trade of Gazprom shares easier within Russia, Ivanov said, since Gazprom would give up its right of first refusal to buy shares on "organised markets."

But he said it was still unclear whether Russia's main stockmarket, the Russian Trading System, an over-the-counter type market which is generally not considered "organised," would be included in the list.
